I mean to follow thee. Let me think:
306I would wish your Grace to feign a pilgrimage
307To Our Lady of Loretto, scarce seven leagues
308From fair Ancona, so may you depart
309Your country with more honour, and your flight
310Will seem a princely progress, retaining
311Your usual train about you.

DUCHESS.

Your usual train about you. Sir, your direction
312Shall lead me, by the hand.

CARIOLA.

Shall lead me, by the hand. In my opinion,
313She were better progress to the baths at Lucca,
314Or go visit the Spa
315In Germany: for, if you will believe me,
316I do not like this jesting with religion,
317This feigned pilgrimage.

DUCHESS.

This feigned pilgrimage. Thou art a superstitious fool:
318Prepare us instantly for our departure.
319Past sorrows, let us moderately lament them,
320For those to come, seek wisely to prevent them.

Exit [Dutchess with Cariola].

BOSOLA.

321A politician is the devil’s quilted anvil,
322He fashions all sins on him, and the blows
323Are never heard; he may work in a lady’s chamber,
324As here for proof. What rests, but I reveal
325All to my lord? Oh, this base quality
326Of intelligencer! Why, every quality i’th’ world
327Prefers but gain, or commendation:
328Now for this act, I am certain to be raised,
329And men that paint weeds, to the life, are praised.

Exit.

Scene iii

[Enter] Cardinal, Ferdinand, Malateste, Pescara, Silvio, Delio.

CARDINAL.

1Must we turn soldier, then?

MALATESTE.

Must we turn soldier, then? The Emperor,
2Hearing your worth that way, ere you attained
3This reverend garment, joins you in commission
4With the right fortunate soldier, the Marquis of Pescara
5And the famous Lannoy.

CARDINAL.

And the famous Lannoy. He that had the honour
6Of taking the French king prisoner?

MALATESTE.

Of taking the French king prisoner? The same.
7Here’s a plot drawn for a new fortification
8At Naples.

FERDINAND.

At Naples. This great Count Malateste, I perceive
9Hath got employment?

DELIO.

Hath got employment? No employment, my lord,
10A marginal note in the muster book, that he is
11A voluntary lord.

FERDINAND.

A voluntary lord. He’s no soldier?

DELIO.

12He has worn gunpowder, in’s hollow tooth,
13For the tooth-ache.

SILVIO.

14He comes to the leaguer with a full intent
15To eat fresh beef, and garlic; means to stay
16Till the scent be gone, and straight return to court.

DELIO.

17He hath read all the late service,
18As the City chronicle relates it,
19And keeps two painters going, only to express
20Battles in model.

SILVIO.

Battles in model. Then he’ll fight by the book.

DELIO.

Battles in model. Then he’ll fight by the book. By the almanac, I think,
21To choose good days, and shun the critical.
22That’s his mistress’ scarf.

SILVIO.

That’s his mistress’ scarf. Yes, he protests
23He would do much for that taffeta,―

DELIO.

24I think he would run away from a battle
25To save it from taking prisoner.

SILVIO.

To save it from taking prisoner. He is horribly afraid
26Gunpowder will spoil the perfume on’t,―

DELIO.

27I saw a Dutchman break his pate once
28For calling him pot-gun; he made his head
29Have a bore in’t, like a musket.

SILVIO.

30I would he had made a touch-hole to’t.
31He is indeed a guarded sumpter-cloth
32Only for the remove of the court.

[Enter Bosola.]

PESCARA.

33Bosola arrived? What should be the business?
34Some falling out amongst the cardinals?
35These factions amongst great men, they are like
36Foxes, when their heads are divided:
37They carry fire in their tails, and all the country
38About them goes to wrack for’t.

SILVIO.

About them goes to wrack for’t. What’s that Bosola?

DELIO.

I knew him in Padua, a fantastical scholar, like
such who study to know how many knots was in Hercules’
club; of what colour Achilles’ beard was, or whether Hector
were not troubled with the toothache. He hath studied
himself half blear-eyed, to know the true symmetry of
Caesar’s nose by a shoeing-horn: and this he did to gain the
name of a speculative man.

PESCARA.

46Mark Prince Ferdinand,
47A very salamander lives in’s eye,
48To mock the eager violence of fire.

SILVIO.

That cardinal hath made more bad faces with his
oppression than ever Michael Angelo made good ones: he
lifts up’s nose, like a foul porpoise before a storm,―

PESCARA.

52The Lord Ferdinand laughs.

DELIO.

53Like a deadly cannon, that lightens ere it smokes.

PESCARA.

54These are your true pangs of death,
55The pangs of life, that struggle with great statesmen,―

DELIO.

In such a deformed silence, witches whisper their
charms.

CARDINAL.

58Doth she make religion her riding hood
59To keep her from the sun and tempest?

FERDINAND.

To keep her from the sun and tempest? That:
60That damns her. Methinks her fault and beauty
61Blended together, show like leprosy,
62The whiter, the fouler. I make it a question
63Whether her beggarly brats were ever christened.

CARDINAL.

64I will instantly solicit the state of Ancona
65To have them banished.

FERDINAND.

To have them banished. You are for Loretto?
66I shall not be at your ceremony; fare you well:
67Write to the Duke of Malfi, my young nephew
68She had by her first husband, and acquaint him
69With's mother's honesty.

BOSOLA.

With's mother's honesty. I will.

FERDINAND.

With's mother's honesty. I will. Antonio!
70A slave, that only smelled of ink and counters,
71And nev’r in’s life looked like a gentleman,
72But in the audit time: go, go presently,
73Draw me out an hundred and fifty of our horse,
74And meet me at the fort-bridge.

Exeunt.

Scene iv

[Enter] two Pilgrims to the Shrine of Our Lady of Loretto.

1 PILGRIM.

1I have not seen a goodlier shrine than this,
2Yet I have visited many.

2 PILGRIM.

Yet I have visited many. The Cardinal of Aragon
3Is this day to resign his cardinal’s hat;
4His sister duchess likewise is arrived
5To pay her vow of pilgrimage. I expect
6A noble ceremony.

1 PILGRIM.

7No question.—They come.

Here the ceremony of the Cardinal's instalment in the habit of a soldier: performed in delivering up his cross, hat, robes, and ring at the shrine; and investing him with sword, helmet, shield, and spurs. Then Antonio, the Duchess, and their children, having presented themselves at the shrine, are (by a form of banishment in dumb-show expressed towards them by the Cardinal, and the state of Ancona) banished. During all which ceremony this ditty is sung to very solemn music, by divers churchmen; and then

Exeunt.

Arms and honours deck thy story, / To thy fame’s eternal glory, / Adverse fortune ever fly thee, / No disastrous fate come nigh thee. / I alone will sing thy praises, / Whom to honour virtue raises; / And thy study, that divine is, / Bent to martial discipline is: / Lay aside all those robes lie by thee, / Crown thy arts with arms: they’ll beautify thee. / O worthy of worthiest name, adorned in this manner, / Lead bravely thy forces on, under war’s warlike banner: / O mayst thou prove fortunate in all martial courses, / Guide thou still by skill, in arts and forces: / Victory attend thee nigh, whilst fame sings loud thy powers, / Triumphant conquest crown thy head, and blessings pour down showers.

1 PILGRIM.

8Here’s a strange turn of state: who would have thought
9So great a lady would have matched herself
10Unto so mean a person? Yet the Cardinal
11Bears himself much too cruel.

2 PILGRIM.

Bears himself much too cruel. They are banished.

1 PILGRIM.

12But I would ask, what power hath this state
13Of Ancona, to determine of a free prince?

2 PILGRIM.

14They are a free state sir, and her brother showed
15How that the Pope, forehearing of her looseness,
16Hath seized into th’ protection of the Church
17The dukedom which she held as dowager.

1 PILGRIM.

18But by what justice?

2 PILGRIM.

But by what justice? Sure I think by none,
19Only her brother’s instigation.

1 PILGRIM.

20What was it, with such violence he took
21Off from her finger?

2 PILGRIM.

Off from her finger? ’Twas her wedding-ring,
22Which he vowed shortly he would sacrifice
23To his revenge.

1 PILGRIM.

To his revenge. Alas Antonio!
24If that a man be thrust into a well,
25No matter who sets hand to’t, his own weight
26Will bring him sooner to th’ bottom. Come, let’s hence
27Fortune makes this conclusion general,
28All things do help th’unhappy man to fall.

Exeunt.

Scene v

[Enter] Antonio, Duchess, Children, Cariola, Servants.

DUCHESS.

1Banished Ancona?

ANTONIO.

Banished Ancona? Yes, you see what power
2Lightens in great men’s breath.

DUCHESS.

Lightens in great men’s breath. Is all our train
3Shrunk to this poor remainder?

ANTONIO.

Shrunk to this poor remainder? These poor men,
4Which have got little in your service, vow
5To take your fortune. But your wiser buntings,
6Now they are fledged, are gone.

DUCHESS.

Now they are fledged, are gone. They have done wisely;
7This puts me in mind of death: physicians thus,
8With their hands full of money, use to give o’er
9Their patients.

ANTONIO.

Their patients. Right the fashion of the world:
10From decayed fortunes every flatterer shrinks,
11Men cease to build where the foundation sinks.

DUCHESS.

12I had a very strange dream tonight.

ANTONIO.

I had a very strange dream tonight. What was’t?

DUCHESS.

13Methought I wore my coronet of state,
14And on a sudden all the diamonds
15Were changed to pearls.

ANTONIO.

Were changed to pearls. My interpretation
16Is, you’ll weep shortly; for to me, the pearls
17Do signify your tears.

DUCHESS.

Do signify your tears. The birds, that live i’th’ field
18On the wild benefit of nature, live
19Happier than we; for they may choose their mates,
20And carol their sweet pleasures to the spring.

[Enter Bosola with a letter which he presents to the Dutchess.]

BOSOLA.

21You are happily o’ertane.

DUCHESS.

You are happily o’ertane. From my brother?

BOSOLA.

22Yes, from the Lord Ferdinand; your brother,
23All love, and safety―

DUCHESS.

All love, and safety― Thou dost blanch mischief;
24Wouldst make it white. See, see; like to calm weather
25At sea before a tempest, false hearts speak fair
26To those they intend most mischief.
27[She reads] A Letter: Send Antonio to me; I want his head in a business.
28(A politic equivocation)
29He doth not want your counsel, but your head;
30That is, he cannot sleep till you be dead.
31And here’s another pitfall, that’s strewed o’er
32With roses: mark it, ’tis a cunning one:

I stand engaged for your husband for several debts at Naples:
let not that trouble him, I had rather have his heart than his
money.

36And I believe so too.

BOSOLA.

And I believe so too. What do you believe?

DUCHESS.

37That he so much distrusts my husband’s love,
38He will by no means believe his heart is with him
39Until he see it. The devil is not cunning enough
40To circumvent us in riddles.

BOSOLA.

41Will you reject that noble and free league
42Of amity and love which I present you?

DUCHESS.

43Their league is like that of some politic kings,
44Only to make themselves of strength and power
45To be our after-ruin: tell them so.

BOSOLA.

46And what from you?

ANTONIO.

And what from you? Thus tell him: I will not come.

BOSOLA.

47And what of this?

ANTONIO.

And what of this? My brothers have dispersed
48Bloodhounds abroad; which till I hear are muzzled,
49No truce, though hatched with ne’er such politic skill,
50Is safe, that hangs upon our enemies’ will.
51I’ll not come at them.

BOSOLA.

I’ll not come at them. This proclaims your breeding.
52Every small thing draws a base mind to fear;
53As the adamant draws iron: fare you well sir,
54You shall shortly hear from’s.

Exit.

DUCHESS.

You shall shortly hear from’s. I suspect some ambush:
55Therefore by all my love; I do conjure you
56To take your eldest son, and fly towards Milan;
57Let us not venture all this poor remainder
58In one unlucky bottom.

ANTONIO.

In one unlucky bottom. You counsel safely.
59Best of my life, farewell. Since we must part,
60Heaven hath a hand in’t: but no otherwise
61Than as some curious artist takes in sunder
62A clock, or watch, when it is out of frame,
63To bring’t in better order.

DUCHESS.

To bring’t in better order. I know not which is best,
64To see you dead, or part with you. Farewell boy,
65Thou art happy, that thou hast not understanding
66To know thy misery. For all our wit
67And reading brings us to a truer sense
68Of sorrow. In the eternal Church, sir,
69I do hope we shall not part thus.

ANTONIO.

I do hope we shall not part thus. O be of comfort,
70Make patience a noble fortitude:
71And think not how unkindly we are used.
72Man, like to cassia, is proved best, being bruised.

DUCHESS.

73Must I like to a slave-born Russian,
74Account it praise to suffer tyranny?
75And yet, O Heaven, thy heavy hand is in’t.
76I have seen my little boy oft scourge his top,
77And compared myself to’t: nought made me e’er go right,
78But Heaven’s scourge-stick.

ANTONIO.

But Heaven’s scourge-stick. Do not weep:
79Heaven fashioned us of nothing; and we strive
80To bring ourselves to nothing. Farewell Cariola,
81[To the Dutchess] If I do never see thee more, And thy sweet armful.
82Be a good mother to your little ones,
83And save them from the tiger: fare you well.

DUCHESS.

84Let me look upon you once more: for that speech
85Came from a dying father: your kiss is colder
86Than that I have seen an holy anchorite
87Give to a dead man’s skull.

ANTONIO.

88My heart is turned to a heavy lump of lead,
89With which I sound my danger: fare you well.

Exit [with elder son.]

DUCHESS.

90My laurel is all withered.

CARIOLA.

91Look, Madam, what a troop of armèd men
92Make toward us.

Enter Bosola with a guard [vizarded].

DUCHESS.

Make toward us. O, they are very welcome:
93When Fortune’s wheel is over-charged with princes,
94The weight makes it move swift. I would have my ruin
95Be sudden. I am your adventure, am I not?

BOSOLA.

96You are: you must see your husband no more,―

DUCHESS.

97What devil art thou, that counterfeits Heaven’s thunder?

BOSOLA.

98Is that terrible? I would have you tell me whether
99Is that note worse that frights the silly birds
100Out of the corn; or that which doth allure them
101To the nets? You have hearkened to the last too much.

DUCHESS.

102O misery! like to a rusty o’ercharged cannon,
103Shall I never fly in pieces? Come: to what prison?

BOSOLA.

104To none.

DUCHESS.

To none. Whither then?

BOSOLA.

To none. Whither then? To your palace.

DUCHESS.

105I have heard that Charon’s boat serves to convey
106All o’er the dismal lake, but brings none back again.

BOSOLA.

107Your brothers mean you safety and pity.

DUCHESS.

108Pity!
109With such a pity men preserve alive
110Pheasants and quails, when they are not fat enough
111To be eaten.

BOSOLA.

112These are your children?

DUCHESS.

These are your children? Yes.

BOSOLA.

These are your children? Yes. Can they prattle?

DUCHESS.

113No:
114But I intend, since they were born accursed;
115Curses shall be their first language.

BOSOLA.

Curses shall be their first language. Fie, madam!
116Forget this base, low fellow.

DUCHESS.

Forget this base, low fellow. Were I a man,
117I’ll’d beat that counterfeit face into thy other―

BOSOLA.

118One of no birth.

DUCHESS.

One of no birth. Say that he was born mean,
119Man is most happy, when’s own actions
120Be arguments and examples of his virtue.

BOSOLA.

121A barren, beggarly virtue.

DUCHESS.

122I prithee, who is greatest, can you tell?
123Sad tales befit my woe: I'll tell you one.
124A Salmon, as she swam unto the sea,
125Met with a Dog-fish; who encounters her
126With this rough language: ‘Why art thou so bold
127To mix thyself with our high state of floods
128Being no eminent courtier, but one
129That for the calmest and fresh time o’th’ year
130Dost live in shallow rivers, rank’st thyself
131With silly Smelts and Shrimps? And darest thou
132Pass by our Dog-ship without reverence?’
133‘O’, quoth the Salmon, ‘sister, be at peace:
134Thank Jupiter, we both have passed the Net,
135Our value never can be truly known,
136Till in the Fisher’s basket we be shown;
137I’th’ Market then my price may be the higher,
138Even when I am nearest to the Cook, and fire.
139So, to great men, the moral may be stretched.
140Men oft are valued high, when they’re most wretch’d.
141But come: whither you please. I am armed ’gainst misery:
142Bent to all sways of the oppressors’ will.
143There’s no deep valley, but near some great hill.

Ex[eunt.]

Act IV

Scene i

[Enter Ferdinand and Bosola]

FERDINAND.

1How doth our sister Duchess bear herself
2In her imprisonment?

BOSOLA.

In her imprisonment? Nobly: I’ll describe her:
3She’s sad, as one long used to’t: and she seems
4Rather to welcome the end of misery
5Than shun it: a behaviour so noble,
6As gives a majesty to adversity:
7You may discern the shape of loveliness
8More perfect in her tears, than in her smiles;
9She will muse four hours together: and her silence,
10Methinks, expresseth more than if she spake.

FERDINAND.

11Her melancholy seems to be fortified
12With a strange disdain.

BOSOLA.

With a strange disdain. ’Tis so: and this restraint
13(Like English mastives, that grow fierce with tying)
14Makes her too passionately apprehend
15Those pleasures she’s kept from.

FERDINAND.

Those pleasures she’s kept from. Curse upon her!
16I will no longer study in the book
17Of another’s heart: inform her what I told you.

Exit.

[Bosola draws the traverse to reveal the Dutchess, Cariola and Servants.]

BOSOLA.

18All comfort to your Grace;―

DUCHESS.

All comfort to your Grace;― I will have none.
19’Pray-thee, why dost thou wrap thy poisoned pills
20In gold and sugar?

BOSOLA.

21Your elder brother the Lord Ferdinand
22Is come to visit you: and sends you word
23’Cause once he rashly made a solemn vow
24Never to see you more; he comes i’th’ night;
25And prays you, gently, neither torch nor taper
26Shine in your chamber: he will kiss your hand;
27And reconcile himself: but, for his vow,
28He dares not see you.

DUCHESS.

He dares not see you. At his pleasure.
29Take hence the lights: he’s come.

[Exeunt servants with lights; enter Ferdinand.]

FERDINAND.

30Where are you?

DUCHESS.

Where are you? Here, sir.

FERDINAND.

31This darkness suits you well.

DUCHESS.

This darkness suits you well. I would ask you pardon.

FERDINAND.

32You have it;
33For I account it the honourabl’st revenge
34Where I may kill, to pardon: where are your cubs?

DUCHESS.

35Whom?

FERDINAND.

36Call them your children;
37For though our national law distinguish bastards
38From true legitimate issue, compassionate nature
39Makes them all equal.

DUCHESS.

Makes them all equal. Do you visit me for this?
40You violate a sacrament o’th’ Church
41Shall make you howl in hell for’t.

FERDINAND.

Shall make you howl in hell for’t. It had been well,
42Could you have lived thus always, for indeed
43You were too much i’th’ light. But no more;
44I come to seal my peace with you: here’s a hand,
45(gives her a dead man’s hand.) To which you have vowed much love: the ring upon’t
46You gave.

DUCHESS.

You gave. I affectionately kiss it.

FERDINAND.

47Pray do: and bury the print of it in your heart.
48I will leave this ring with you, for a love-token:
49And the hand, as sure as the ring: and do not doubt
50But you shall have the heart too. When you need a friend
51Send it to him that owed it: you shall see
52Whether he can aid you.

DUCHESS.

Whether he can aid you. You are very cold.
53I fear you are not well after your travel:
54Ha? Lights: Oh horrible!

FERDINAND.

55Let her have lights enough.

[Exit.

[Enter servants with lights.]

DUCHESS.

56What witchcraft doth he practice, that he hath left
57A dead man’s hand here?―

Here is discovered, behind a traverse, the artificial figures of Antonio and his children; appearing as if they were dead.

BOSOLA.

58Look you: here’s the piece from which ’twas tane;
59He doth present you this sad spectacle,
60That now you know directly they are dead,
61Hereafter you may, wisely, cease to grieve
62For that which cannot be recovered.

DUCHESS.

63There is not between heaven and earth one wish
64I stay for after this: it wastes me more,
65Than were’t my picture, fashioned out of wax,
66Stuck with a magical needle, and then buried
67In some foul dunghill: And yond’s an excellent property
68For a tyrant, which I would account mercy,―

BOSOLA.

69What’s that?

DUCHESS.

70If they would bind me to that lifeless trunk,
71And let me freeze to death.

BOSOLA.

And let me freeze to death. Come, you must live.

DUCHESS.

72That’s the greatest torture souls feel in hell,
73In hell: that they must live, and cannot die.
74Portia, I’ll new kindle thy coals again,
75And revive the rare and almost dead example
76Of a loving wife.

BOSOLA.

Of a loving wife. O fie! despair? remember
77You are a Christian.

DUCHESS.

You are a Christian. The Church enjoins fasting:
78I’ll starve myself to death.

BOSOLA.

I’ll starve myself to death. Leave this vain sorrow;
79Things being at the worst, begin to mend:
80The bee when he hath shot his sting into your hand
81May then play with your eyelid.

DUCHESS.

May then play with your eyelid. Good comfortable fellow
82Persuade a wretch that’s broke upon the wheel
83To have all his bones new set: entreat him live,
84To be executed again. Who must dispatch me?
85I account this world a tedious theatre,
86For I do play a part in’t ’gainst my will.

BOSOLA.

87Come, be of comfort, I will save your life.

DUCHESS.

88Indeed I have not leisure to tend so small a business.

BOSOLA.

89Now, by my life, I pity you.

DUCHESS.

Now, by my life, I pity you. Thou art a fool then,
90To waste thy pity on a thing so wretched
91As cannot pity itself. I am full of daggers.
92Puff! let me blow these vipers from me.

[Enter Servant.]

93What are you?

SERVANT.

What are you? One that wishes you long life.

DUCHESS.

94I would thou wert hanged for the horrible curse
95Thou hast given me: I shall shortly grow one
96Of the miracles of pity. I’ll go pray. No,
97I’ll go curse.

BOSOLA.

I’ll go curse. Oh, fie!

DUCHESS.

98I could curse the stars.

BOSOLA.

I could curse the stars. Oh, fearful!

DUCHESS.

99And those three smiling seasons of the year
100Into a Russian winter: nay the world
101To its first chaos.

BOSOLA.

102Look you, the stars shine still.

DUCHESS.

Look you, the stars shine still. Oh, but you must
103Remember, my curse hath a great way to go:
104Plagues, that make lanes through largest families,
105Consume them.

BOSOLA.

Consume them. Fie lady!

DUCHESS.

Consume them. Fie lady! Let them like tyrants
106Never be remembered, but for the ill they have done:
107Let all the zealous prayers of mortified
108Churchmen forget them,―

BOSOLA.

Churchmen forget them,― O uncharitable!

DUCHESS.

109Let Heaven, a little while, cease crowning martyrs,
110To punish them.
111Go, howl them this: and say I long to bleed.
112It is some mercy when men kill with speed.

Exit [with servants]

[Enter Ferdinand. ]

FERDINAND.

113Excellent; as I would wish: she’s plagued in art.
114These presentations are but framed in wax
115By the curious master in that quality,
116Vincentio Lauriola, and she takes them
117For true substantial bodies.

BOSOLA.

For true substantial bodies. Why do you do this?

FERDINAND.

118To bring her to despair.

BOSOLA.

To bring her to despair. ’Faith, end here;
119And go no farther in your cruelty,
120Send her a penitential garment, to put on
121Next to her delicate skin, and furnish her
122With beads and prayer books.

FERDINAND.

With beads and prayer books. Damn her! that body of hers,
123While that my blood ran pure in’t, was more worth
124Than that which thou wouldst comfort, called a soul.
125I will send her masques of common courtesans,
126Have her meat served up by bawds and ruffians,
127And, ’cause she’ll needs be mad, I am resolved
128To remove forth the common hospital
129All the mad folk, and place them near her lodging:
130There let them practice together, sing, and dance,
131And act their gambols to the full o’th’ moon:
132If she can sleep the better for it, let her.
133Your work is almost ended.

BOSOLA.

Your work is almost ended. Must I see her again?

FERDINAND.

134Yes.

BOSOLA.

Yes. Never.

FERDINAND.

Yes. Never. You must.

BOSOLA.

Yes. Never. You must. Never in mine own shape;
135That’s forfeited by my intelligence,
136And this last cruel lie: when you send me next,
137The business shall be comfort.

FERDINAND.

The business shall be comfort. Very likely:
138Thy pity is nothing of kin to thee. Antonio
139Lurks about Milan; thou shalt shortly thither,
140To feed a fire as great as my revenge,
141Which nev’r will slack, till it have spent his fuel;
142Intemperate agues make physicians cruel

Exeunt.

Scene ii

[Enter Duchess and Cariola.]

DUCHESS.

1What hideous noise was that?

CARIOLA.

What hideous noise was that? ’Tis the wild consort
2Of madmen, lady, which your tyrant brother
3Hath placed about your lodging. This tyranny,
4I think, was never practiced till this hour.

DUCHESS.

5Indeed I thank him: nothing but noise, and folly
6Can keep me in my right wits, whereas reason
7And silence make me stark mad. Sit down,
8Discourse to me some dismal tragedy.

CARIOLA.

9O ’twill increase your melancholy.

DUCHESS.

O ’twill increase your melancholy. Thou art deceived;
10To hear of greater grief would lessen mine.
11This is a prison?

CARIOLA.

This is a prison? Yes, but you shall live
12To shake this durance off.

DUCHESS.

To shake this durance off. Thou art a fool:
13The robin red-breast and the nightingale
14Never live long in cages.

CARIOLA.

Never live long in cages. Pray dry your eyes.
15What think you of Madam?

DUCHESS.

What think you of Madam? Of nothing:
16When I muse thus, I sleep.

CARIOLA.

17Like a madman, with your eyes open?

DUCHESS.

18Dost thou think we shall know one another
19In th’other world?

CARIOLA.

In th’other world? Yes, out of question.

DUCHESS.

20O that it were possible we might
21But hold some two days’ conference with the dead,
22From them I should learn somewhat, I am sure
23I never shall know here. I'll tell thee a miracle,
24I am not mad yet, to my cause of sorrow.
25Th’heaven o'er my head seems made of molten brass,
26The earth of flaming sulphur, yet I am not mad.
27I am acquainted with sad misery,
28As the tanned galley-slave is with his oar.
29Necessity makes me suffer constantly.
30And custom makes it easy. Who do I look like now?

CARIOLA.

31Like to your picture in the gallery,
32A deal of life in show, but none in practice:
33Or rather like some reverend monument
34Whose ruins are even pitied.

DUCHESS.

Whose ruins are even pitied. Very proper:
35And Fortune seems only to have her eyesight,
36To behold my tragedy.
37How now! what noise is that?

[Enter] Servant.

SERVANT.

How now! what noise is that? I am come to tell you,
38Your brother hath intended you some sport.
39A great physician when the Pope was sick
40Of a deep melancholy, presented him
41With several sorts of madmen, which wild object,
42Being full of change and sport, forced him to laugh,
43And so th’impostume broke: the selfsame cure
44The Duke intends on you.

DUCHESS.

The Duke intends on you. Let them come in.

SERVANT.

45There's a mad lawyer, and a secular priest,
46A doctor that hath forfeited his wits
47By jealousy; an astrologian,
48That in his works said such a day o’th’ month
49Should be the day of doom; and, failing of’t,
50Ran mad; an English tailor, crazed i’th’ brain
51With the study of new fashion; a gentleman usher
52Quite beside himself with care to keep in mind
53The number of his lady's salutations,
54Or ‘How do you?’ she employed him in each morning:
55A farmer too, an excellent knave in grain,
56Mad, 'cause he was hindered transportation;
57And let one broker, that’s mad, loose to these,
58You'ld think the devil were among them.

DUCHESS.

59Sit Cariola: let them loose when you please,
60For I am chained to endure all your tyranny.

[Enter Madmen.]

Here, by a madman, this song is sung to a dismal kind of music. / O let us howl, some heavy note, / Some deadly-doggèd howl, / Sounding, as from the threat’ning of beasts, and fatal fowl. / As ravens, screech-owls, bulls, and bears, / We’ll bill, and bawl our parts, / Till yerksome noise, have cloyed your ears, / and corrosived your hearts. / At last when as our choir wants breath, / our bodies being blest, / We’ll sing like swans, to welcome death, / and die in love and rest. throat,

MAD ASTROLOGER.

Doomsday not come yet? I’ll draw it
nearer by a perspective, or make a glass, that shall set all the
world on fire upon an instant. I cannot sleep, my pillow is
stufft with a litter of porcupines.

MAD LAWYER.

Hell is a mere glass-house, where the devils
are continually blowing up women’s souls on hollow irons,
and the fire never goes out.

MAD PRIEST.

I will lie with every woman in my parish
the tenth night: I will tithe them over like haycocks.

MAD DOCTOR.

Shall my pothecary outgo me, because I am
a cuckold? I have found out his roguery: he makes allum of
his wife’s urine, and sells it to Puritans, that have sore
throats with over-straining.

MAD ASTROLOGER.

I have skill in heraldry.

MAD LAWYER.

Hast?

MAD ASTROLOGER.

You do give for your crest a woodcock’s
head, with the brains picked out on’t. You are a very ancient
gentleman.

MAD PRIEST.

Greek is turned Turk; we are only to be saved
by the Helvetian translation.

MAD ASTROLOGER

[to lawyer]. Come on sir, I will lay the
law to you.

MAD LAWYER.

Oh, rather lay a corrosive, the law will eat
to the bone.

MAD PRIEST.

He that drinks but to satisfy nature is damned.

MAD DOCTOR.

If I had my glass here, I would show a sight
should make all the women here call me mad doctor.

MAD ASTROLOGER

[pointing to the Priest]. What’s he, a rope-
maker?

MAD LAWYER.

No, no, no, a snuffling knave, that while he
shows the tombs, will have his hand in a wench’s placket.

MAD PRIEST.

Woe to the caroche that brought home my
wife from the masque, at three o’clock in the morning; it
had a large featherbed in it.

MAD DOCTOR.

I have pared the devil’s nails forty times,
roasted them in ravens’ eggs, and cured agues with them.

MAD PRIEST.

Get me three hundred milch bats, to make
possets to procure sleep.

MAD DOCTOR.

All the college may throw their caps at me, I
have made a soap-boiler costive: it was my masterpiece:―

Here the dance, consisting of 8. madmen, with music answerable thereunto, after which Bosola, like an old man, enters.

DUCHESS.

101Is he mad too?

SERVANT.

Is he mad too? Pray question him; I'll leave you.

[Exeunt Servant and Madmen]

BOSOLA.

102I am come to make thy tomb.

DUCHESS.

I am come to make thy tomb. Ha! my tomb?
103Thou speak’st as if I lay upon my death-bed,
104Gasping for breath: dost thou perceive me sick?

BOSOLA.

Yes, and the more dangerously, since thy sickness is insensible.

DUCHESS.

Thou art not mad, sure; dost know me?

BOSOLA.

Yes.

DUCHESS.

Who am I?

BOSOLA.

Thou art a box of worm seed, at best, but a sal-
vatory of green mummy: what’s this flesh? a little cruded
milk, fantastical puff-paste: our bodies are weaker than those
paper prisons boys use to keep flies in: more contemptible;
since ours is to preserve earth-worms: didst thou ever see
a lark in a cage? such is the soul in the body: this world
is like her little turf of grass, and the heaven o’er our heads,
like her looking-glass, only gives us a miserable knowledge
of the small compass of our prison.

DUCHESS.

Am not I thy Duchess?

BOSOLA.

Thou art some great woman, sure; for riot begins
to sit on thy forehead (clad in gray hairs) twenty years sooner
than on a merry milkmaid’s. Thou sleep’st worse, than if a
mouse should be forced to take up her lodging in a cat’s ear:
a little infant, that breeds its teeth, should it lie with thee,
would cry out as if thou wert the more unquiet bedfellow.

DUCHESS.

I am Duchess of Malfi still.

BOSOLA.

That makes thy sleeps so broken:

127Glories, like glow-worms, afar off shine bright,
128But looked to near, have neither heat nor light.

DUCHESS.

Thou art very plain.

BOSOLA.

My trade is to flatter the dead, not the living;
I am a tomb-maker.

DUCHESS.

And thou com’st to make my tomb?

BOSOLA.

Yes.

DUCHESS.

134Let me be a little merry;
135Of what stuff wilt thou make it?

BOSOLA.

136Nay, resolve me first, of what fashion?

DUCHESS.

Why, do we grow fantastical in our death-bed?
Do we affect fashion in the grave?

BOSOLA.

139Most ambitiously. Princes’ images on their tombs
140Do not lie as they were wont, seeming to pray
141Up to Heaven: but with their hands under their cheeks,
142As if they died of the tooth-ache; they are not carved
143With their eyes fixed upon the stars; but as
144Their minds were wholly bent upon the world,
145The self-same way they seem to turn their faces.

DUCHESS.

146Let me know fully therefore the effect
147Of this thy dismal preparation,
148This talk, fit for a charnel.

BOSOLA.

This talk, fit for a charnel. Now I shall;

[Enter Executioners with] a coffin, cords, and a bell.

149Here is a present from your princely brothers,
150And may it arrive welcome, for it brings
151Last benefit, last sorrow.

DUCHESS.

Last benefit, last sorrow. Let me see it.
152I have so much obedience, in my blood,
153I wish it in their veins, to do them good.

BOSOLA.

154This is your last presence chamber.

CARIOLA.

155O my sweet lady!

DUCHESS.

O my sweet lady! Peace; it affrights not me.

BOSOLA.

156I am the common bellman,
157That usually is sent to condemned persons,
158The night before they suffer.

DUCHESS.

The night before they suffer. Even now thou said’st
159Thou wast a tomb-maker?

BOSOLA.

Thou wast a tomb-maker? ’Twas to bring you
160By degrees to mortification. Listen:
161[rings the bell] Hark, now everything is still,
162The screech-owl and the whistler shrill
163Call upon our Dame, aloud,
164And bid her quickly don her shroud.
165Much you had of land and rent,
166Your length in clay’s now competent.
167A long war disturbed your mind,
168Here your perfect peace is signed.
169Of what is’t fools make such vain keeping?
170Sin their conception, their birth, weeping:
171Their life, a general mist of error,
172Their death, a hideous storm of terror.
173Strew your hair with powders sweet:
174Don clean linen, bath your feet,
175And, the foul fiend more to check,
176A crucifix let bless your neck.
177’Tis now full tide ’tween night and day,
178End your groan, and come away.

[Executioners approach.]

CARIOLA.

179Hence villains, tyrants, murderers. Alas!
180What will you do with my lady? Call for help.

DUCHESS.

181To whom, to our next neighbours? They are mad-folks.

BOSOLA.

182Remove that noise.

[Executioners seize Cariola, who struggles.]

DUCHESS.

Remove that noise. Farewell Cariola,
183In my last will I have not much to give;
184A many hungry guests have fed upon me,
185Thine will be a poor reversion.

CARIOLA.

Thine will be a poor reversion. I will die with her.

DUCHESS.

186I pray thee, look thou giv’st my little boy
187Some syrup for his cold, and let the girl
188Say her prayers, ere she sleep.

[Cariola is forced off.]

Say her prayers, ere she sleep. Now, what you please,
189What death?

BOSOLA.

What death? Strangling: here are your executioners.

DUCHESS.

190I forgive them:
191The apoplexy, catarrh, or cough o'th’ lungs
192Would do as much as they do.

BOSOLA.

193Doth not death fright you?

DUCHESS.

Doth not death fright you? Who would be afraid on’t?
194Knowing to meet such excellent company
195In th’other world?

BOSOLA.

In th’other world? Yet, methinks,
196The manner of your death should much afflict you,
197This cord should terrify you?

DUCHESS.

This cord should terrify you? Not a whit:
198What would it pleasure me, to have my throat cut
199With diamonds? or to be smothered
200With cassia? or to be shot to death, with pearls?
201I know death hath ten thousand several doors
202For men to take their Exits: and ’tis found
203They go on such strange geometrical hinges,
204You may open them both ways: any way, for Heaven sake,
205So I were out of your whispering. Tell my brothers
206That I perceive death, now I am well awake,
207Best gift is, they can give, or I can take.
208I would fain put off my last woman's fault,
209I’ll’d not be tedious to you.

EXECUTIONERS.

I’ll’d not be tedious to you. We are ready.

DUCHESS.

210Dispose my breath how please you, but my body
211Bestow upon my women, will you?

EXECUTIONERS.

Bestow upon my women, will you? Yes.

DUCHESS.

212Pull, and pull strongly, for your able strength
213Must pull down heaven upon me:
214Yet stay, heaven gates are not so highly arched
215As princes’ palaces: they that enter there
216Must go upon their knees. Come violent death,
217Serve for mandragora to make me sleep;
218Go tell my brothers, when I am laid out,
219They then may feed in quiet.

They strangle her.

BOSOLA.

They then may feed in quiet. Where's the waiting woman?
220Fetch her. Some other strangle the children.

[Exeunt Executioners. Enter one with Cariola.]

221Look you, there sleeps your mistress.

CARIOLA.

Look you, there sleeps your mistress. O you are damned
222Perpetually for this. My turn is next,
223Is’t not so ordered?

BOSOLA.

Is’t not so ordered? Yes, and I am glad
224You are so well prepared for’t.

CARIOLA.

You are so well prepared for’t. You are deceived sir,
225I am not prepared for't. I will not die,
226I will first come to my answer; and know
227How I have offended.

BOSOLA.

How I have offended. Come, dispatch her.
228You kept her counsel, now you shall keep ours.

CARIOLA.

229I will not die, I must not, I am contracted
230To a young gentleman.

EXECUTIONER

To a young gentleman. [showing the noose]. Here’s your wedding-ring.

CARIOLA.

231Let me but speak with the Duke. I'll discover
232Treason to his person.

BOSOLA.

Treason to his person. Delays: throttle her.

EXECUTIONER.

233She bites: and scratches.

CARIOLA.

She bites: and scratches. If you kill me now
234I am damned. I have not been at confession
235This two years.

BOSOLA.

This two years. When!

CARIOLA.

236I am quick with child.

BOSOLA.

I am quick with child. Why then,
237Your credit’s saved: bear her into th' next room.
238Let this lie still.

[Executioners strangle Cariola and exeunt with her body.

Enter Ferdinand.]

FERDINAND.

239Is she dead?

BOSOLA.

Is she dead? She is what
240You’ll’d have her. But here begin your pity,

[Bosola draws the traverse and] Shows the children strangled.

241Alas, how have these offended?

FERDINAND.

Alas, how have these offended? The death
242Of young wolves is never to be pitied.

BOSOLA.

243Fix your eye here.

FERDINAND.

Fix your eye here. Constantly.

BOSOLA.

Fix your eye here. Constantly. Do you not weep?
244Other sins only speak; murther shrieks out:
245The element of water moistens the earth,
246But blood flies upwards, and bedews the heavens.

FERDINAND.

247Cover her face. Mine eyes dazzle: she died young.

BOSOLA.

248I think not so: her infelicity
249Seemed to have years too many.

FERDINAND.

Seemed to have years too many. She and I were twins:
250And should I die this instant, I had lived
251Her time to a minute.

BOSOLA.

Her time to a minute. It seems she was born first:
252You have bloodily approved the ancient truth,
253That kindred commonly do worse agree
254Than remote strangers.

FERDINAND.

Than remote strangers. Let me see her face again.
255Why didst not thou pity her? What an excellent
256Honest man might’st thou have been
257If thou hadst borne her to some sanctuary!
258Or, bold in a good cause, opposed thyself
259With thy advanced sword above thy head,
260Between her innocence and my revenge!
261I bade thee, when I was distracted of my wits,
262Go kill my dearest friend, and thou hast done’t.
263For let me but examine well the cause;
264What was the meanness of her match to me?
265Only I must confess, I had a hope,
266Had she continued widow, to have gained
267An infinite mass of treasure by her death:
268And that was the main cause; her marriage,
269That drew a stream of gall quite through my heart;
270For thee, (as we observe in tragedies
271That a good actor many times is cursed
272For playing a villain’s part) I hate thee for't:
273And, for my sake, say thou hast done much ill, well.

BOSOLA.

274Let me quicken your memory: for I perceive
275You are falling into ingratitude. I challenge
276The reward due to my service.

FERDINAND.

The reward due to my service. I'll tell thee,
277What I'll give thee—

BOSOLA.

What I'll give thee— Do.

FERDINAND.

What I'll give thee— Do. I'll give thee a pardon
278For this murder.

BOSOLA.

For this murder. Ha?

FERDINAND.

For this murder. Ha? Yes: and ’tis
279The largest bounty I can study to do thee.
280By what authority didst thou execute
281This bloody sentence?

BOSOLA.

This bloody sentence? By yours.

FERDINAND.

This bloody sentence? By yours. Mine? Was I her judge?
282Did any ceremonial form of law
283Doom her to not-being? did a complete jury
284Deliver her conviction up i’th’ court?
285Where shalt thou find this judgement registered
286Unless in hell? See: like a bloody fool
287Th’hast forfeited thy life, and thou shalt die for't.

BOSOLA.

288The office of justice is perverted quite
289When one thief hangs another: who shall dare
290To reveal this?

FERDINAND.

To reveal this? Oh, I'll tell thee:
291The wolf shall find her grave, and scrape it up;
292Not to devour the corpse, but to discover
293The horrid murther.

BOSOLA.

The horrid murther. You; not I shall quake for't.

FERDINAND.

294Leave me.

BOSOLA.

Leave me. I will first receive my pension.

FERDINAND.

295You are a villain.

BOSOLA.

You are a villain. When your ingratitude
296Is judge, I am so―

FERDINAND.

Is judge, I am so― O horror!
297That not the fear of Him which binds the devils
298Can prescribe man obedience.
299Never look upon me more.

BOSOLA.

Never look upon me more. Why fare thee well:
300Your brother and yourself are worthy men;
301You have a pair of hearts are hollow graves,
302Rotten, and rotting others: and your vengeance,
303Like two chained bullets, still goes arm in arm;
304You may be brothers: for treason, like the plague,
305Doth take much in a blood. I stand like one
306That long hath tane a sweet and golden dream.
307I am angry with myself, now that I wake.

FERDINAND.

308Get thee into some unknown part o’th’ world
309That I may never see thee.

BOSOLA.

That I may never see thee. Let me know
310Wherefore I should be thus neglected? Sir,
311I served your tyranny: and rather strove
312To satisfy yourself, than all the world;
313And though I loathed the evil, yet I loved
314You that did counsel it: and rather sought
315To appear a true servant than an honest man.

FERDINAND.

316I'll go hunt the badger by owl-light:
317'Tis a deed of darkness. Exit.

BOSOLA.

318He’s much distracted. Off my painted honour!
319While with vain hopes our faculties we tire,
320We seem to sweat in ice and freeze in fire;
321What would I do, were this to do again?
322I would not change my peace of conscience
323For all the wealth of Europe. She stirs; here’s life.
324Return, fair soul, from darkness, and lead mine
325Out of this sensible hell. She’s warm, she breathes:
326Upon thy pale lips I will melt my heart
327To store them with fresh colour. Who’s there?
328Some cordial drink! Alas! I dare not call:
329So pity would destroy pity: her eye opes,
330And heaven in it seems to ope, that late was shut,
331To take me up to mercy.

DUCHESS.

To take me up to mercy. Antonio!

BOSOLA.

332Yes, Madam, he is living,
333The dead bodies you saw were but feigned statues;
334He’s reconciled to your brothers: the Pope hath wrought
335The atonement.

DUCHESS.

The atonement. Mercy.

she dies.

BOSOLA.

336Oh, she’s gone again: there the cords of life broke.
337Oh sacred innocence, that sweetly sleeps
338On turtles’ feathers: whilst a guilty conscience
339Is a black register, wherein is writ
340All our good deeds and bad; a perspective
341That shows us hell; that we cannot be suffered
342To do good when we have a mind to it!
343This is manly sorrow:
344These tears, I am very certain, never grew
345In my mother’s milk. My estate is sunk
346Below the degree of fear: where were
347These penitent fountains while she was living?
348Oh, they were frozen up: here is a sight
349As direful to my soul as is the sword
350Unto a wretch hath slain his father. Come,
351I’ll bear thee hence,
352And execute thy last will; that’s deliver
353Thy body to the reverend dispose
354Of some good women: that the cruel tyrant
355Shall not deny me. Then I’ll post to Milan,
356Where somewhat I will speedily enact
357Worth my dejection.

Exit [carrying the body].

Act V

Scene i

[Enter Antonio and Delio.]

ANTONIO.

1What think you of my hope of reconcilement
2To the Aragonian brethren?

DELIO.

To the Aragonian brethren? I misdoubt it
3For though they have sent their letters of safe conduct
4For your repair to Milan, they appear
5But nets to entrap you. The Marquis of Pescara,
6Under whom you hold certain land in cheat,
7Much ’gainst his noble nature, hath been moved
8To sieze those lands, and some of his dependents
9Are at this instant making it their suit
10To be invested in your revenues.
11I cannot think they mean well to your life,
12That do deprive you of your means of life,
13Your living.

ANTONIO.

Your living. You are still an heretic.
14To any safety I can shape myself.

DELIO.

15Here comes the Marquis. I will make myself
16Petitioner for some part of your land,
17To know whither it is flying.

ANTONIO.

To know whither it is flying. I pray, do.

[Enter Pescara.]

DELIO.

18Sir, I have a suit to you.

PESCARA.

Sir, I have a suit to you. To me?

DELIO.

Sir, I have a suit to you. To me? An easy one:
19There is the citadel of St. Bennet,
20With some demesnes, of late in the possession
21Of Antonio Bologna; please you bestow them on me?

PESCARA.

22You are my friend. But this is such a suit
23Nor fit for me to give, nor you to take.

DELIO.

24No sir?

PESCARA.

No sir? I will give you ample reason for’t
25Soon, in private. Here’s the Cardinal’s mistress.

[Enter Julia.]

JULIA.

26My lord, I am grown your poor petitioner,
27And should be an ill beggar, had I not
28A great man’s letter here, the Cardinal’s,
29To court you in my favour.

[She gives him a letter which he reads.]

PESCARA.

To court you in my favour. He entreats for you
30The citadel of Saint Bennet, that belonged
31To the banished Bologna.

JULIA.

To the banished Bologna. Yes.

PESCARA.

32I could not have thought of a friend I could
33Rather pleasure with it: ’tis yours.

JULIA.

Rather pleasure with it: ’tis yours. Sir, I thank you:
34And he shall know how doubly I am engaged
35Both in your gift, and speediness of giving,
36Which makes your grant the greater.

Exit.

ANTONIO.

37[aside]. How they fortifyaparte
38Themselves with my ruin!

DELIO.

Themselves with my ruin! Sir, I am
39Little bound to you.

PESCARA.

Little bound to you. Why?

DELIO.

40Because you denied this suit to me, and gave’t
41To such a creature.

PESCARA.

To such a creature. Do you know what it was?
42It was Antonio’s land: not forfeited
43By course of law; but ravished from his throat
44By the Cardinal’s entreaty: it were not fit
45I should bestow so main a piece of wrong
46Upon my friend: ’tis a gratification
47Only due to a strumpet; for it is injustice.
48Shall I sprinkle the pure blood of innocents
49To make those followers I call my friends
50Look ruddier upon me? I am glad
51This land, tane from the owner by such wrong,
52Returns again unto so foul an use,
53As salary for his lust. Learn, good Delio,
54To ask noble things of me, and you shall find
55I’ll be a noble giver.

DELIO.

I’ll be a noble giver. You instruct me well.

ANTONIO.

56[aside]. Why, here’s a man, now, would fright impudenceaparte
57From sauciest beggars.

PESCARA.

From sauciest beggars. Prince Ferdinand’s come to Milan
58Sick, as they give out, of an apoplexy:
59But some say ’tis a frenzy; I am going
60Exit. To visit him.

ANTONIO.

Exit. To visit him. 'Tis a noble old fellow:

DELIO.

61What course do you mean to take, Antonio?

ANTONIO.

62This night I mean to venture all my fortune,
63Which is no more than a poor ling’ring life,
64To the Cardinal’s worst of malice. I have got
65Private access to his chamber: and intend
66To visit him, about the mid of night,
67As once his brother did our noble Duchess.
68It may be that the sudden apprehension
69Of danger (for I’ll go in mine own shape)
70When he shall see it fraught with love and duty,
71May draw the poison out of him, and work
72A friendly reconcilement: if it fail,
73Yet it shall rid me of this infamous calling,
74For better fall once, than be ever falling.

DELIO.

75I’ll second you in all danger: and, howe’er,
76My life keeps rank with yours.

ANTONIO.

77You are still my lovèd and best friend.

Exeunt.

Scene ii

[Enter Pescara and Doctor]

PESCARA.

1Now doctor, may I visit your patient?

DOCTOR.

2If’t please your lordship: but he’s instantly
3To take the air here in the gallery,
4By my direction.

PESCARA.

By my direction. Pray thee, what’s his disease?

DOCTOR.

5A very pestilent disease, my lord,
6They call lycanthropia.

PESCARA.

They call lycanthropia. What’s that?
7I need a dictionary to’t.

DOCTOR.

I need a dictionary to’t. I’ll tell you.
8In those that are possessed with’t there o'erflows
9Such melancholy humour, they imagine
10Themselves to be transformèd into wolves.
11Steal forth to churchyards in the dead of night,
12And dig dead bodies up: as two nights since
13One met the Duke, ’bout midnight in a lane
14Behind St. Mark’s church, with the leg of a man
15Upon his shoulder; and he howled fearfully:
16Said he was a wolf: only the difference
17Was, a wolf’s skin was hairy on the outside,
18His on the inside: bade them take their swords,
19Rip up his flesh, and try: straight I was sent for,
20And having ministered to him, found his Grace
21Very well recovered.

PESCARA.

Very well recovered. I am glad on’t.

DOCTOR.

22Yet not without some fear
23Of a relapse: if he grow to his fit again
24I’ll go a nearer way to work with him
25Than ever Paracelsus dreamed of. If
26They’ll give me leave, I’ll buffet his madness out of him.
27Stand aside: he comes.

[Enter Cardinal, Ferdinand, Malateste and Bosola, who remains in the background.]

FERDINAND.

Leave me.

MALATESTE.

Why doth your lordship love this solitariness?

FERDINAND.

Eagles commonly fly alone. They are crows,
daws, and starlings that flock together. Look, what’s that
follows me?

MALATESTE.

Nothing, my lord.

FERDINAND.

Yes.

MALATESTE.

’Tis your shadow.

FERDINAND.

Stay it; let it not haunt me.

MALATESTE.

Impossible, if you move, and the sun shine.

FERDINAND.

I will throttle it.

[Throws himself upon his shadow. ]

MALATESTE.

Oh, my lord: you are angry with nothing.

FERDINAND.

You are a fool. How is’t possible I should
catch my shadow unless I fall upon’t? When I go to hell, I
mean to carry a bribe: for look you, good gifts evermore
make way for the worst persons.

PESCARA.

Rise, good my lord.

FERDINAND.

I am studying the art of patience.

PESCARA.

’Tis a noble virtue;―

FERDINAND.

To drive six snails before me, from this town
to Moscow; neither use goad nor whip to them, but let
them take their own time: (the patient’st man i’th’ world
match me for an experiment!) and I’ll crawl after like a
sheep-biter.

CARDINAL.

Force him up.

[They get Ferdinand to his feet.]

FERDINAND.

53Use me well, you were best.
54What I have done, I have done: I’ll confess nothing.

DOCTOR.

55Now let me come to him. Are you mad, my lord?
56Are you out of your princely wits?

FERDINAND.

Are you out of your princely wits? What’s he?

PESCARA.

Are you out of your princely wits? What’s he? Your doctor.

FERDINAND.

57Let me have his beard sawed off, and his eyebrows
58Filed more civil.

DOCTOR.

Filed more civil. I must do mad tricks with him,
59For that’s the only way on’t. I have brought
60Your Grace a salamander’s skin, to keep you
61From sun-burning.

FERDINAND.

From sun-burning. I have cruel sore eyes.

DOCTOR.

62The white of a cockatrice’s egg is present remedy.

FERDINAND.

63Let it be a new-laid one, you were best.
64Hide me from him. Physicians are like kings,
65They brook no contradiction.

DOCTOR.

They brook no contradiction. Now he begins
66To fear me; now let me alone with him.

[Ferdinand tries to take off his gown; Cardinal seizes him.]

CARDINAL.

67How now, put off your gown?

DOCTOR.

Let me have some forty urinals filled with rose-
water: he and I’ll go pelt one another with them; now he
begins to fear me. Can you fetch a frisk, sir?
[aside to Cardinal] Let him go, let him go upon my peril. I find by
his eye, he stands in awe of me: I’ll make him as tame as a
dormouse.

[Cardinal releases Ferdinand.]

FERDINAND.

Can you fetch your frisks, sir! I will stamp him
into a cullis; flay off his skin, to cover one of the anatomies,
this rogue hath set i’th’ cold yonder, in Barber-Chirur-
geons’ Hall. Hence, hence! you are all of you like beasts for
[throws the Doctor down and beats him] there’s sacrifice,
nothing left of you, but tongue and belly, flattery and lechery.

[Exit.]

PESCARA.

Doctor, he did not fear you throughly.

DOCTOR.

True, I was somewhat too forward.

BOSOLA.

82[aside]. Mercy upon me, what a fatal judgementaparte
83Hath fall’n upon this Ferdinand!

PESCARA.

Hath fall’n upon this Ferdinand! Knows your Grace
84What accident hath brought unto the Prince
85This strange distraction?

CARDINAL

86[aside]. I must feign somewhat. Thus they say it grew:aparte
87You have heard it rumored for these many years,
88None of our family dies, but there is seen
89The shape of an old woman, which is given
90By tradition, to us, to have been murthered
91By her nephews, for her riches. Such a figure
92One night, as the Prince sat up late at’s book,
93Appeared to him; when crying out for help,
94The gentlemen of's chamber found his Grace
95All on a cold sweat, altered much in face
96And language. Since which apparition
97He hath grown worse and worse, and I much fear
98He cannot live.

BOSOLA.

99Sir, I would speak with you.

PESCARA.

Sir, I would speak with you. We’ll leave your Grace,
100Wishing to the sick Prince, our noble lord,
101All health of mind and body.

CARDINAL.

All health of mind and body. You are most welcome.

[Exeunt Pescara, Malateste and Doctor.]

102[aside] Are you come? So: this fellow must not knowaparte
103By any means I had intelligence
104In our Duchess’ death. For, though I counseled it,
105The full of all th’engagement seemed to grow
106From Ferdinand. Now sir, how fares our sister?
107I do not think but sorrow makes her look
108Like to an oft-dyed garment. She shall now
109Taste comfort from me: why do you look so wildly?
110Oh, the fortune of your master here, the Prince,
111Dejects you, but be you of happy comfort:
112If you’ll do one thing for me I'll entreat,
113Though he had a cold tombstone o’er his bones,
114I’ll’d make you what you would be.

BOSOLA.

I’ll’d make you what you would be. Any thing;
115Give it me in a breath, and let me fly to’t:
116They that think long, small expedition win,
117For musing much o’th’ end, cannot begin.

[Enter] Julia.

JULIA.

118Sir, will you come in to supper?

CARDINAL.

Sir, will you come in to supper? I am busy, leave me.

JULIA.

119[aside]. What an excellent shape hath that fellow!aparte

Exit.

CARDINAL.

120’Tis thus: Antonio lurks here in Milan;
121Inquire him out, and kill him: while he lives
122Our sister cannot marry, and I have thought
123Of an excellent match for her: do this, and style me
124Thy advancement.

BOSOLA.

Thy advancement. But by what means shall I find him out?

CARDINAL.

125There is a gentleman, called Delio
126Here in the camp, that hath been long approved
127His loyal friend. Set eye upon that fellow,
128Follow him to mass; may be Antonio,
129Although he do account religion
130But a school-name, for fashion of the world,
131May accompany him: or else go inquire out
132Delio’s confessor, and see if you can bribe
133Him to reveal it: there are a thousand ways
134A man might find to trace him: as, to know
135What fellows haunt the Jews for taking up
136Great sums of money, for sure he’s in want;
137Or else to go to th’ picture-makers and learn
138Who brought her picture lately: some of these
139Happily may take—

BOSOLA.

Happily may take— Well, I’ll not freeze i’th’ business,
140I would see that wretched thing, Antonio,
141Above all sights i’th’ world.

CARDINAL.

Above all sights i’th’ world. Do, and be happy.

Exit.

BOSOLA.

142This fellow doth breed basilisks in’s eyes,
143He’s nothing else but murder: yet he seems
144Not to have notice of the Duchess’ death.
145’Tis his cunning: I must follow his example;
146There cannot be a surer way to trace,
147Than that of an old fox.

[Enter Julia with a pistol.]

JULIA.

Than that of an old fox. So, sir, you are well met.

BOSOLA.

148How now?

JULIA.

How now? Nay, the doors are fast enough.
149Now, sir, I will make you confess your treachery.

BOSOLA.

150Treachery?

JULIA.

Treachery? Yes. Confess to me
151Which of my women ’twas you hired to put
152Love-powder into my drink?

BOSOLA.

Love-powder into my drink? Love-powder?

JULIA.

153Yes, when I was at Malfi;
154Why should I fall in love with such a face else?
155I have already suffered for thee so much pain,
156The only remedy to do me good
157Is to kill my longing.

BOSOLA.

Is to kill my longing. Sure, your pistol holds
158Nothing but perfumes or kissing-comfits: excellent lady,
159You have a pretty way on’t to discover
160Your longing. Come, come, I’ll disarm you
161And arm you thus: [embraces her] yet this is wondrous strange.

JULIA.

162Compare thy form and my eyes together,
163You’ll find my love no such great miracle.
164[Kisses him] Now you’ll say
165I am wanton. This nice modesty in ladies
166Is but a troublesome familiar
167That haunts them.

BOSOLA.

168Know you me, I am a blunt soldier.

JULIA.

Know you me, I am a blunt soldier. The better:
169Sure, there wants fire where there are no lively sparks
170Of roughness.

BOSOLA.

Of roughness. And I want compliment.

JULIA.

Of roughness. And I want compliment. Why, ignorance
171In courtship cannot make you do amiss,
172If you have a heart to do well.

BOSOLA.

If you have a heart to do well. You are very fair.

JULIA.

173Nay, if you lay beauty to my charge,
174I must plead unguilty.

BOSOLA.

I must plead unguilty. Your bright eyes
175Carry a quiver of darts in them, sharper
176Than sunbeams.

JULIA.

Than sunbeams. You will mar me with commendation,
177Put yourself to the charge of courting me,
178Whereas now I woo you.

BOSOLA.

179[aside]. I have it, I will work upon this creature,aparte
180Let us grow most amorously familiar.
181If the great Cardinal now should see me thus,
182Would he not count me a villain?

JULIA.

183No, he might count me a wanton,
184Not lay a scruple of offense on you:
185For if I see, and steal a diamond,
186The fault is not i’th’ stone, but in me the thief
187That purloins it. I am sudden with you;
188We that are great women of pleasure, use to cut off
189These uncertain wishes and unquiet longings,
190And in an instant join the sweet delight
191And the pretty excuse together: had you been i’th’ street,
192Under my chamber window, even there
193I should have courted you.

BOSOLA.

I should have courted you. Oh, you are an excellent lady.

JULIA.

194Bid me do somewhat for you presently
195To express I love you.

BOSOLA.

To express I love you. I will, and if you love me,
196Fail not to effect it.
197The Cardinal is grown wondrous melancholy,
198Demand the cause, let him not put you off
199With feigned excuse; discover the main ground on’t.

JULIA.

200Why would you know this?

BOSOLA.

Why would you know this? I have depended on him,
201And I hear that he is fall’n in some disgrace
202With the Emperor: if he be, like the mice
203That forsake falling houses, I would shift
204To other dependence.

JULIA.

205You shall not need follow the wars:
206I’ll be your maintenance.

BOSOLA.

207And I your loyal servant;
208But I cannot leave my calling.

JULIA.

But I cannot leave my calling. Not leave an
209Ungrateful general for the love of a sweet lady?
210You are like some, cannot sleep in feather-beds,
211But must have blocks for their pillows.

BOSOLA.

But must have blocks for their pillows. Will you do this?

JULIA.

212Cunningly.

BOSOLA.

Cunningly. Tomorrow I’ll expect th’intelligence.

JULIA.

213Tomorrow? get you into my cabinet,
214You shall have it with you: do not delay me,
215No more than I do you. I am like one
216That is condemned: I have my pardon promised,
217But I would see it sealed. Go, get you in,
218You shall see me wind my tongue about his heart
219Like a skein of silk.

[Bosola withdraws behind the traverse; enter Cardinal.]

CARDINAL.

Like a skein of silk. Where are you?

[Enter servants]

SERVANT.

220Here.

CARDINAL.

Here. Let none upon your lives
221Have conference with the Prince Ferdinand,
222Unless I know it.
Unless I know it. [aside] In this distractionaparte
223He may reveal the murther.

[Exeunt servants.]

224Yond’s my ling’ring consumption:
225I am weary of her; and by any means
226Would be quit of―

JULIA.

Would be quit of― How now, my Lord?
227What ails you?

CARDINAL.

What ails you? Nothing.

JULIA.

What ails you? Nothing. Oh, you are much altered:
228Come, I must be your secretary, and remove
229This lead from off your bosom; what’s the matter?

CARDINAL.

230I may not tell you.

JULIA.

I may not tell you. Are you so far in love with sorrow,
231You cannot part with part of it? or think you
232I cannot love your Grace when you are sad,
233As well as merry? or do you suspect
234I, that have been a secret to your heart
235These many winters, cannot be the same
236Unto your tongue?

CARDINAL.

Unto your tongue? Satisfy thy longing.
237The only way to make thee keep my counsel
238Is not to tell thee.

JULIA.

Is not to tell thee. Tell your echo this,
239Or flatterers, that, like echoes, still report
240What they hear, though most imperfect, and not me:
241For, if that you be true unto yourself,
242I’ll know.

CARDINAL.

I’ll know. Will you rack me?

JULIA.

I’ll know. Will you rack me? No, judgement shall
243Draw it from you. It is an equal fault,
244To tell one’s secrets unto all, or none.

CARDINAL.

245The first argues folly.

JULIA.

The first argues folly. But the last tyranny.

CARDINAL.

246Very well; why, imagine I have committed
247Some secret deed which I desire the world
248May never hear of!

JULIA.

May never hear of! Therefore may not I know it?
249You have concealed for me as great a sin
250As adultery. Sir, never was occasion
251For perfect trial of my constancy
252Till now. Sir, I beseech you.

CARDINAL.

Till now. Sir, I beseech you. You’ll repent it.

JULIA.

Till now. Sir, I beseech you. You’ll repent it. Never.

CARDINAL.

253It hurries thee to ruin: I’ll not tell thee.
254Be well advised, and think what danger ’tis
255To receive a prince’s secrets: they that do,
256Had need have their breasts hooped with adamant
257To contain them. I pray thee yet be satisfied,
258Examine thine own frailty; ’tis more easy
259To tie knots, than unloose them: ’tis a secret
260That, like a ling’ring poison, may chance lie
261Spread in thy veins, and kill thee seven year hence.

JULIA.

262Now you dally with me.

CARDINAL.

Now you dally with me. No more; thou shalt know it.
263By my appointment the great Duchess of Malfi
264And two of her young children, four nights since
265Were strangled.

JULIA.

Were strangled. Oh Heaven! Sir, what have you done?

CARDINAL.

266How now? how settles this? Think you your bosom
267Will be a grave dark and obscure enough
268For such a secret?

JULIA.

For such a secret? You have undone yourself, sir.

CARDINAL.

269Why?

JULIA.

Why? It lies not in me to conceal it.

CARDINAL.

Why? It lies not in me to conceal it. No?
270Come, I will swear you to’t upon this book.

JULIA.

271Most religiously.

CARDINAL.

Most religiously. Kiss it.

[She kisses a Bible.]

272Now you shall never utter it; thy curiosity
273Hath undone thee; thou’rt poisoned with that book.
274Because I knew thou couldst not keep my counsel,
275I have bound thee to't by death.

[Enter Bosola]

BOSOLA.

276For pity-sake, hold.

CARDINAL.

For pity-sake, hold. Ha, Bosola!

JULIA.

For pity-sake, hold. Ha, Bosola! I forgive you
277This equal piece of justice you have done:
278For I betrayed your counsel to that fellow;
279He overheard it; that was the cause I said
280It lay not in me to conceal it.

BOSOLA.

It lay not in me to conceal it. Oh foolish woman,
281Couldst not thou have poisoned him?

JULIA.

Couldst not thou have poisoned him? ’Tis weakness,
282Too much to think what should have been done. I go,
283I know not whither.

[Dies.]

CARDINAL.

I know not whither. Wherefore com’st thou hither?

BOSOLA.

284That I might find a great man, like yourself,
285Not out of his wits, as the Lord Ferdinand,
286To remember my service.

CARDINAL.

To remember my service. I’ll have thee hewed in pieces.

BOSOLA.

287Make not yourself such a promise of that life
288Which is not yours to dispose of.

CARDINAL.

Which is not yours to dispose of. Who placed thee here?

BOSOLA.

289Her lust, as she intended.

CARDINAL.

Her lust, as she intended. Very well;
290Now you know me for your fellow murderer.

BOSOLA.

291And wherefore should you lay fair marble colours
292Upon your rotten purposes to me?
293Unless you imitate some that do plot great treasons,
294And when they have done, go hide themselves i’th' graves
295Of those were actors in't?

CARDINAL.

296No more: there is a fortune attends thee.

BOSOLA.

297Shall I go sue to Fortune any longer?
298’Tis the fool's pilgrimage.

CARDINAL.

’Tis the fool's pilgrimage. I have honours in store for thee.

BOSOLA.

299There are a many ways that conduct to seeming
300Honour, and some of them very dirty ones.

CARDINAL.

301Throw to the devil
302Thy melancholy; the fire burns well,
303What need we keep a stirring of’t, and make
304A greater smother? Thou wilt kill Antonio?

BOSOLA.

305Yes.

CARDINAL.

Yes. Take up that body.

BOSOLA.

Yes. Take up that body. I think I shall
306Shortly grow the common bier for churchyards!

CARDINAL.

307I will allow thee some dozen of attendants,
308To aid thee in the murther.

BOSOLA.

Oh, by no means: physicians that apply horse-
leeches to any rank swelling, use to cut off their tails, that
the blood may run through them the faster. Let me have no
train, when I go to shed blood, lest it make me have a greater,
when I ride to the gallows.

CARDINAL.

314Come to me after midnight, to help to remove that body
315To her own lodging. I’ll give out she died o'th' plague;
316'Twill breed the less inquiry after her death.

BOSOLA.

317Where's Castruchio her husband?

CARDINAL.

318He's rode to Naples to take possession
319Of Antonio's citadel.

BOSOLA.

320Believe me, you have done a very happy turn.

CARDINAL.

321Fail not to come. There is the master-key
322Of our lodgings: and by that you may conceive
323What trust I plant in you.

Exit.

BOSOLA.

What trust I plant in you. You shall find me ready.
324Oh poor Antonio, Though nothing be so needful
325To thy estate, as pity, yet I find
326Nothing so dangerous. I must look to my footing;
327In such slippery ice-pavements, men had need
328To be frost-nailed well: they may break their necks else.
329The president's here afore me: how this man
330Bears up in blood! seems fearless! Why, 'tis well:
331Security some men call the suburbs of hell,
332Only a dead wall between. Well, good Antonio,
333I'll seek thee out; and all my care shall be
334To put thee into safety from the reach
335Of these most cruel biters, that have got
336Some of thy blood already. It may be,
337I'll join with thee in a most just revenge.
338The weakest arm is strong enough, that strikes
339With the sword of justice. Still methinks the Duchess
340Haunts me: there, there: ’tis nothing but my melancholy.
341O penitence, let me truly taste thy cup,
342That throws men down, only to raise them up!

Exit.

Scene iii

[Enter Antonio and Delio; there is an ] echo (from the Duchess’s grave).

DELIO.

1Yond's the Cardinal's window. This fortification
2Grew from the ruins of an ancient abbey:
3And to yond side o'th' river lies a wall,
4Piece of a cloister, which in my opinion
5Gives the best echo that you ever heard;
6So hollow, and so dismal, and withal
7So plain in the distinction of our words,
8That many have supposed it is a spirit
9That answers.

ANTONIO.

That answers. I do love these ancient ruins:
10We never tread upon them, but we set
11Our foot upon some reverend history,
12And, questionless, here in this open court,
13Which now lies naked to the injuries
14Of stormy weather, some men lie interred
15Loved the church so well, and gave so largely to’t,
16They thought it should have canopied their bones
17Till doomsday. But all things have their end:
18Churches and cities, which have diseases like to men
19Must have like death that we have.

ECHO.

Must have like death that we have. Like death that we have.

DELIO.

20Now the echo hath caught you.

ANTONIO.

21It groaned, methought, and gave
22A very deadly accent!

ECHO.

A very deadly accent! Deadly accent.

DELIO.

23I told you ’twas a pretty one. You may make it
24A huntsman, or a falconer, a musician
25Or a thing of sorrow.

ECHO.

Or a thing of sorrow. A thing of sorrow.

ANTONIO.

26Ay, sure: that suits it best.

ECHO.

Ay, sure: that suits it best. That suits it best.

ANTONIO.

27’Tis very like my wife's voice.

ECHO.

’Tis very like my wife's voice. Ay, wife's voice.

DELIO.

28Come: let us walk farther from’t:
29I would not have you go to th’ Cardinal’s tonight:
30Do not.

ECHO.

Do not. Do not.

DELIO.

31Wisdom doth not more moderate wasting sorrow
32Than time: take time for’t: be mindful of thy safety.

ECHO.

33Be mindful of thy safety.

ANTONIO.

Be mindful of thy safety. Necessity compels me:
34Make scrutiny throughout the passes
35Of your own life; you’ll find it impossible
36To fly your fate.

ECHO.

To fly your fate. O fly your fate.

DELIO.

37Hark: the dead stones seem to have pity on you
38And give you good counsel.

ANTONIO.

And give you good counsel. Echo, I will not talk with thee;
39For thou art a dead thing.

ECHO.

For thou art a dead thing. Thou art a dead thing.

ANTONIO.

40My Duchess is asleep now,
41And her little ones, I hope sweetly: oh Heaven
42Shall I never see her more?

ECHO.

Shall I never see her more? Never see her more.

ANTONIO.

43I marked not one repetition of the Echo
44But that: and on the sudden, a clear light
45Presented me a face folded in sorrow.

DELIO.

46Your fancy; merely.

ANTONIO.

Your fancy; merely. Come: I’ll be out of this ague;
47For to live thus, is not indeed to live:
48It is a mockery, and abuse of life.
49I will not henceforth save myself by halves;
50Lose all, or nothing.

DELIO.

Lose all, or nothing. Your own virtue save you.
51I’ll fetch your eldest son; and second you:
52It may be that the sight of his° own blood
53Spread in so sweet a figure, may beget
54The more compassion.

ANTONIO.

The more compassion. However, fare you well.
55Though in our miseries Fortune have a part
56Yet, in our noble suff’rings, she hath none:
57Contempt of pain, that we may call our own

Exe[unt].

Scene iv

[Enter] Cardinal, Pescara, Malateste, Roderigo, Grisolan.

CARDINAL.

1You shall not watch tonight by the sick Prince;
2His Grace is very well recoverèd.

MALATESTE.

3Good my lord, suffer us.

CARDINAL.

Good my lord, suffer us. Oh, by no means:
4The noise and change of object in his eye
5Doth more distract him. I pray, all to bed,
6And though you hear him in his violent fit,
7Do not rise, I entreat you.

PESCARA.

Do not rise, I entreat you. So sir, we shall not―

CARDINAL.

8Nay, I must have you promise
9Upon your honours, for I was enjoined to’t
10By himself; and he seemed to urge it sensibly.

PESCARA.

11Let our honours bind this trifle.

CARDINAL.

12Nor any of your followers.

MALATESTE.

Nor any of your followers. Neither.

CARDINAL.

13It may be, to make trial of your promise
14When he’s asleep, myself will rise, and feign
15Some of his mad tricks, and cry out for help,
16And feign myself in danger.

MALATESTE.

And feign myself in danger. If your throat were cutting,
17I’ll’d not come at you, now I have protested against it.

CARDINAL.

18Why, I thank you.

[Withdraws]

GRISOLAN.

Why, I thank you. ’Twas a foul storm tonight.

RODERIGO.

19The Lord Ferdinand’s chamber shook like an osier.

MALATESTE.

20’Twas nothing but pure kindness in the devil,
21To rock his own child.

Exeunt [Roderigo, Malataste, Pescara, Grisolan.]

CARDINAL.

22The reason why I would not suffer these
23About my brother, is because at midnight
24I may with better privacy convey
25Julia’s body to her own lodging. O, my conscience!
26I would pray now: but the devil takes away my heart
27For having any confidence in prayer.
28About this hour I appointed Bosola
29To fetch the body: when he hath served my turn.
30He dies.

Exit. [Enter Bosola.]

BOSOLA.

Ha? ’twas the Cardinals voice. I heard him name
Bosola, and my death: listen, I hear one’s footing.

[Enter Ferdinand.]

FERDINAND.

33Strangling is a very quiet death.

BOSOLA.

34Nay then I see, I must stand upon my guard.

FERDINAND.

35What say’ to that? Whisper, softly: do you agree to’t?
36So it must be done i’th’ dark: the Cardinal
37Would not for a thousand pounds the Doctor should see it.

Exit.

BOSOLA.

38My death is plotted; here’s the consequence of murther.
39We value not desert, nor Christian breath
40When we know black deeds must be cured with death.

[Withdraws. Enter Antonio and a Servant.]

SERVANT.

41Here stay sir, and be confident, I pray:
42I’ll fetch you a dark lanthorn.

Exit.

ANTONIO.

I’ll fetch you a dark lanthorn. Could I take him
43At his prayers, there were hope of pardon.

BOSOLA.

44Fall right my sword: [strikes Antonio down from behind.]
45I’ll not give thee so much leisure as to pray.

ANTONIO.

46Oh, I am gone! Thou hast ended a long suit,
47In a minute.

BOSOLA.

In a minute. What art thou?

ANTONIO.

In a minute. What art thou? A most wretched thing
48That only have thy benefit in death,
49To appear myself.

[Enter Servant with a dark lanthorn.]

SERVANT.

To appear myself. Where are you sir?

ANTONIO.

50Very near my home. Bosola?

SERVANT.

Very near my home. Bosola? Oh misfortune!

BOSOLA.

51[to servant] Smother thy pity, thou art dead else. Antonio?
52The man I would have saved ’bove mine own life!
53We are merely the star’s tennis-balls, struck and banded
54Which way please them: oh good Antonio,
55I’ll whisper one thing in thy dying ear,
56Shall make thy heart break quickly. Thy fair Duchess
57And two sweet children—

ANTONIO.

And two sweet children— Their very names
58Kindle a little life in me.

BOSOLA.

Kindle a little life in me. Are murdered!

ANTONIO.

59Some men have wish’s to die
60At the hearing of sad tidings: I am glad
61That I shall do’t in sadness: I would not now
62Wish my wounds balmed, nor healed: for I have no use
63To put my life to. In all our quest of greatness,
64Like wanton boys, whose pastime is their care,
65We follow after bubbles, blown in th’air.
66Pleasure of life, what is’t? only the good hours
67Of an ague: merely a preparative to rest,
68To endure vexation. I do not ask
69The process of my death: only commend me
70To Delio.

BOSOLA.

71Break, heart!

ANTONIO.

72And let my son fly the courts of princes.

[Dies.]

BOSOLA.

73Thou seem’st to have loved Antonio?

SERVANT.

74I brought him hither,
75To have reconciled him to the Cardinal.

BOSOLA.

76I do not ask thee that.
77Take him up, if thou tender thine own life,
78And bear him where the Lady Julia
79Was wont to lodge. Oh, my fate moves swift.
80I have this Cardinal in the forge already,
81Now I’ll bring him to th’ hammer. (O direful misprision!)
82I will not imitate things glorious,
83No more than base: I’ll be mine own example.
84On, on: and look thou represent, for silence,
85The thing thou bear’st.

Exeunt.

Scene v

[Enter] Cardinal (with a book).

CARDINAL.

1I am puzzled in a question about hell:
2He says, in hell there’s one material fire,
3And yet it shall not burn all men alike.
4Lay him by. How tedious is a guilty conscience!
5When I look into the fishponds, in my garden,
6Methinks I see a thing armed with a rake
7That seems to strike at me. Now? Art thou come?

[Enter Bolosa and Servant with Antonio’s body.]

8Thou look’st ghastly:
9There sits in thy face some great determination,
10Mixed with some fear.

BOSOLA.

Mixed with some fear. Thus it lightens into action:
11I am come to kill thee.

CARDINAL.

I am come to kill thee. Ha? Help! our guard!

BOSOLA.

12Thou art deceived:
13They are out of thy howling.

CARDINAL.

14Hold: and I will faithfully divide
15Revenues with thee.

BOSOLA.

Revenues with thee. Thy prayers and proffers
16Are both unseasonable.

CARDINAL.

Are both unseasonable. Raise the watch:
17We are betrayed!

BOSOLA.

We are betrayed! I have confined your flight:
18I’ll suffer your retreat to Julia’s chamber,
19But no further.

CARDINAL.

But no further. Help: we are betrayed!

[Enter Pescara, Malateste, Roderigo and Grisolan, above.]

MALATESTE.

But no further. Help: we are betrayed! Listen.

CARDINAL.

20My dukedom for rescue!

RODERIGO.

My dukedom for rescue! Fie upon his counterfeiting.

MALATESTE.

21Why, ’tis not the Cardinal.

RODERIGO.

Why, ’tis not the Cardinal. Yes, yes, ’tis he:
22But I’ll see him hanged, ere I’ll go down to him.

CARDINAL.

23Here’s a plot upon me; I am assaulted. I am lost,
24Unless some rescue!

GRISOLAN.

Unless some rescue! He doth this pretty well:
25But it will not serve to laugh me out of mine honour.

CARDINAL.

26The sword’s at my throat!

RODERIGO.

The sword’s at my throat! You would not bawl so loud, then.

MALATESTE.

27Come, come: let’s go to bed: he told us thus much aforehand.

PESCARA.

28He wished you should not come at him: but believe’t,
29The accent of the voice sounds not in jest.
30I’ll down to him, howsoever, and with engines
31[Exit.] Force ope the doors.

RODERIGO.

[Exit.] Force ope the doors. Let’s follow him aloof,
32And note how the Cardinal will laugh at him.

[Exeunt above.]

BOSOLA.

33There’s for you first:
34’Cause you shall not unbarricade the door
35To let in rescue.

He kills the Servant.

CARDINAL.

36What cause hast thou to pursue my life?

BOSOLA.

What cause hast thou to pursue my life? Look there.

CARDINAL.

37Antonio!

BOSOLA.

Antonio! Slain by my hand unwittingly.
38Pray, and be sudden: when thou killed’st thy sister,
39Thou took’st from Justice her most equal balance,
40And left her naught but her sword.

CARDINAL.

And left her naught but her sword. O mercy!

BOSOLA.

41Now it seems thy greatness was only outward:
42For thou fall’st faster of thyself than calamity
43Can drive thee. I’ll not waste longer time. There.

[Stabs the Cardinal.]

CARDINAL.

44Thou hast hurt me!

BOSOLA.

Thou hast hurt me! Again!

[Stabs him again.]

CARDINAL.

45Shall I die like a leveret
46Without any resistance? Help, help, help!
47I am slain!

[Enter] Ferdinand.]

FERDINAND.

I am slain! Th’alarum? give me a fresh horse.
48Rally the vaunt-guard; or the day is lost.
49Yield, yield! I give you the honour of arms,
50Shake my sword over you, will you yield?

CARDINAL.

51Help me, I am your brother.

FERDINAND.

Help me, I am your brother. The devil?
52My brother fight upon the adverse party?

(He wounds the Cardinal and, in the scuffle, gives Bosola his death wound.)

53There flies your ransome.

CARDINAL.

There flies your ransome. Oh Justice:
54I suffer now for what hath former bin
